chunks.title: Left Main Coronary Artery (LMCA) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Left Main Coronary Artery (LMCA)
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
Arises from the left aortic sinus and bifurcates into the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) and Left Circumflex (LCx) arteries.

chunks.title: Left Main Coronary Artery (LMCA) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content: ates into the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) and Left Circumflex (LCx) arteries. Significant narrowing in the LMCA affects blood flow to a large portion of the left ventricle and carries significant prognostic weight.

chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)

chunks.title: Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Artery Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
ding (LAD) Artery
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
Courses down the anterior interventricular groove to supply the anterior myocardial wall, apex, and anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum. Often nicknamed the "widowmaker" when severely narrowed proximally. Major side branches include Diagonal branches (D1, D2) and Septal perforators.

chunks.title: Left Circumflex (LCx) Artery Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Left Circumflex (LCx) Artery
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
Traverses the left atrioventricular groove to supply the lateral and posterior left ventricular myocardium. Major side branches include Obtuse Marginal (OM1, OM2) branches.

chunks.title: Right Coronary Artery (RCA) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Right Coronary Artery (RCA)
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
Originates from the right aortic sinus and supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, inferior left ventricular wall, and the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodal conduction tissue in most individuals.

chunks.title: Right Coronary Artery (RCA) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content: rial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodal conduction tissue in most individuals. Branches include Acute Marginal branches, the Posterior Descending Artery (PDA), and Posterior Lateral branches (PLB). Stenosis in the RCA often causes inferior myocardial ischemia or conduction slowing.

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing)
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
Coronary artery narrowing (stenosis) is quantitatively expressed as a percentage reduction in vessel luminal diameter compared with an adjacent angiographically normal reference segment:

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
l diameter compared with an adjacent angiographically normal reference segment:
- **< 50% Luminal Diameter Reduction (Mild / Non-obstructive)**: Usually does not restrict baseline coronary blood flow or cause exercise-induced myocardial ischemia. Primarily managed through aggressive lifestyle modifications, statin therapy, and cardiovascular risk factor optimization.

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
yle modifications, statin therapy, and cardiovascular risk factor optimization.
- **50% to 69% Luminal Diameter Reduction (Moderate Stenosis)**: Borderline hemodynamic significance. May cause angina symptoms during high physical exertion. Often evaluated further with physiologic tests such as Fractional Flow Reserve (FFR) or Instantaneous Wave-free Ratio (iFR).

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
s such as Fractional Flow Reserve (FFR) or Instantaneous Wave-free Ratio (iFR).
- **70% to 99% Luminal Diameter Reduction (Severe / Hemodynamically Significant Stenosis)**: Restricts coronary flow reserve, frequently precipitating effort angina or ischemic myocardial strain.

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content: w reserve, frequently precipitating effort angina or ischemic myocardial strain. Clinical guidelines recommend evaluation by a cardiovascular specialist for potential revascularization (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention / PCI with stent placement, or Coronary Artery Bypass Graft / CABG) alongside medical therapy.

chunks.title: Coronary Artery Stenosis (Percentage Narrowing) Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
t placement, or Coronary Artery Bypass Graft / CABG) alongside medical therapy.
- **100% Luminal Diameter Reduction (Total Occlusion)**: Complete cessation of antegrade blood flow through the native coronary lumen, characteristic of acute myocardial infarction or chronic total occlusion (CTO).

chunks.title: Treatment and Revascularization Guidelines Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Treatment and Revascularization Guidelines
Category: Cardiology & Interventional Cardiovascular Medicine
- **Optimal Medical Therapy (OMT)**: Antiplatelet agents, lipid-lowering therapies (statins), beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors to prevent atherosclerotic progression.

chunks.title: Treatment and Revascularization Guidelines Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
ins), beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors to prevent atherosclerotic progression.
- **Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI / Angioplasty & Stenting)**: Minimally invasive catheter-guided balloon dilation and drug-eluting stent placement to restore vessel caliber in focal severe obstructions.

chunks.title: Treatment and Revascularization Guidelines Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
eluting stent placement to restore vessel caliber in focal severe obstructions.
- **Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)**: Surgical revascularization utilizing arterial (e.g., internal mammary artery) or venous conduits to bypass diffuse multivessel or complex Left Main coronary disease.

chunks.title: Treatment and Revascularization Guidelines Reference
chunks.source: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: American College of Cardiology (ACC) & American Heart Association (AHA) Joint Guidelines / National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
s conduits to bypass diffuse multivessel or complex Left Main coronary disease.
- **Patient Communication Rule**: Angiogram findings require comprehensive correlation with symptoms (chest tightness, shortness of breath, fatigue), non-invasive stress testing, and ventricular function. Patients should always discuss their exact angiographic percentages and personalized treatment options directly with their cardiologist.

# Complete Blood Count (CBC) Reference Guide

**Source Organization**: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
**URL**: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count/
**Category**: Hematology
**Last Reviewed**: 2024

## Overview
The Complete Blood Count (CBC) is one of the most widely performed routine laboratory blood tests. It measures the quantity, size, and maturity of cellular elements circulating within peripheral blood.

## Key Parameters and Clinical Context

chunks.title: Hemoglobin (Hb) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Hemoglobin (Hb)
Category: Hematology
- **Biological Function**: Iron-rich protein contained within Red Blood Cells (RBCs) responsible for binding and delivering oxygen from lungs to systemic tissues.
- **Typical Adult Reference Range**:
  - Males: 13.8 - 17.2 g/dL
  - Females: 12.1 - 15.1 g/dL

chunks.title: Hemoglobin (Hb) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
lt Reference Range**:
  - Males: 13.8 - 17.2 g/dL
  - Females: 12.1 - 15.1 g/dL
  *(Note: Specific laboratory reference ranges may vary slightly based on analyzer methodology, altitude, and demographic cohorts).*
- **Low Levels (Anemia)**: May arise from iron deficiency, acute or occult blood loss, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, chronic inflammatory states, or bone marrow disorders. Common clinical signs include fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, lightheadedness, and pallor.

chunks.title: Hemoglobin (Hb) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
inical signs include fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, lightheadedness, and pallor.
- **Critical/Panic Thresholds**: Hemoglobin levels below 7.0 g/dL often require prompt hospital or emergency medical evaluation due to compromised systemic oxygenation.

chunks.title: White Blood Cell Count (WBC / Leukocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: White Blood Cell Count (WBC / Leukocytes)
Category: Hematology
- **Biological Function**: Primary defensive cells of the innate and adaptive immune system.
- **Typical Adult Reference Range**: 4,000 - 11,000 /uL (or 4.0 - 11.0 x 10^9 /L).

chunks.title: White Blood Cell Count (WBC / Leukocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
*Typical Adult Reference Range**: 4,000 - 11,000 /uL (or 4.0 - 11.0 x 10^9 /L).
- **Elevated Levels (Leukocytosis)**: Most frequently an expected physiological reaction to bacterial or viral infections, systemic inflammation, severe physical exertion, smoking, or tissue trauma. Marked elevations (>30,000 /uL) require prompt hematological evaluation.

chunks.title: White Blood Cell Count (WBC / Leukocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
rauma. Marked elevations (>30,000 /uL) require prompt hematological evaluation.
- **Depressed Levels (Leukopenia)**: May occur with viral infections, autoimmune conditions, medications (e.g., chemotherapy, immunosuppressants), or bone marrow disorders.

chunks.title: Platelets (Thrombocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)] - Parameter: Platelets (Thrombocytes)
Category: Hematology
- **Biological Function**: Cytoplasmic fragments originating from megakaryocytes that aggregate to form primary hemostatic plugs upon vascular endothelial injury.
- **Typical Adult Reference Range**: 150,000 - 450,000 /uL.

chunks.title: Platelets (Thrombocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
endothelial injury.
- **Typical Adult Reference Range**: 150,000 - 450,000 /uL.
- **Low Levels (Thrombocytopenia)**: Elevated risk of mucosal bleeding, spontaneous petechiae, purpura, or epistaxis. Levels under 50,000 /uL warrant urgent clinical attention.
- **High Levels (Thrombocytosis)**: Often reactive/secondary to iron deficiency, acute infection, or chronic inflammation.

## Important Clinical Disclaimers

chunks.title: Platelets (Thrombocytes) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH) - MedlinePlus & National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
chunks.content:
y, acute infection, or chronic inflammation.

## Important Clinical Disclaimers
Laboratories calibrate reference intervals using specific population statistics. Abnormal values on a CBC must always be interpreted in the context of the patient's comprehensive clinical history, physical examination, and concurrent medications.

chunks.title: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
[American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)] - Parameter: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
Category: Endocrinology & Metabolism
- **Role**: Pituitary hormone responding to negative feedback from circulating free thyroid hormones. Highly sensitive marker of thyroid axis status.
- **Reference Range**: Typically 0.45 - 4.5 mIU/L (may shift with pregnancy or geriatric age).

chunks.title: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
ange**: Typically 0.45 - 4.5 mIU/L (may shift with pregnancy or geriatric age).
- **High TSH**: Primary Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) when Free T4 is low. If Free T4 is normal, it is classified as Subclinical Hypothyroidism. Common symptoms include fatigue, cold sensitivity, constipation, dry skin, and mild unexplained weight gain.

chunks.title: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
ue, cold sensitivity, constipation, dry skin, and mild unexplained weight gain.
- **Low TSH**: Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) when Free T4 is high, or Subclinical Hyperthyroidism if Free T4 is normal. Symptoms include palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, insomnia, and weight loss.

chunks.title: Free Thyroxine (Free T) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
[American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)] - Parameter: Free Thyroxine (Free T)
Category: Endocrinology & Metabolism
- **Reference Range**: Typically 0.8 - 1.8 ng/dL. Unbound, active form of thyroxine.

## Glycemic Profile

chunks.title: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
[American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)] - Parameter: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG)
Category: Endocrinology & Metabolism
- **Normal**: < 100 mg/dL (after at least 8 hours fasting).
- **Impaired Fasting Glucose (Prediabetes)**: 100 - 125 mg/dL.
- **Diabetes Threshold**: >= 126 mg/dL (requires confirmation on repeat testing).

chunks.title: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
**Diabetes Threshold**: >= 126 mg/dL (requires confirmation on repeat testing).
- **Critical Emergency (>300 mg/dL or <50 mg/dL)**: Hypoglycemia (<50 mg/dL) causes neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, diaphoresis, seizure risk). Severe hyperglycemia (>300 mg/dL) carries risk of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state.

chunks.title: Hemoglobin Ac (HbAc) Reference
chunks.source: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.organization: American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)
chunks.content:
[American Thyroid Association (ATA) & American Diabetes Association (ADA)] - Parameter: Hemoglobin Ac (HbAc)
Category: Endocrinology & Metabolism
- **Role**: Reflects average glycemic control over the lifespan of red blood cells (~90-120 days).
- **Normal**: < 5.7%
- **Prediabetes**: 5.7% - 6.4%
- **Diabetes**: >= 6.5%

# Lipid Panel & Cardiovascular Health Guidelines

**Source Organization**: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
**URL**: https://www.cdc.gov/cholesterol/about.html
**Category**: Cardiovascular & Lipidology
**Last Reviewed**: 2024

## Overview
A lipid panel (or lipid profile) assesses circulating concentrations of lipids and lipoproteins. It serves as an essential tool for evaluating long-term atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk.

## Key Parameters

chunks.title: Total Cholesterol Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content:
[American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)] - Parameter: Total Cholesterol
Category: Cardiovascular & Lipidology
- **Desirable**: < 200 mg/dL
- **Borderline High**: 200 - 239 mg/dL
- **High**: >= 240 mg/dL

chunks.title: Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content:
[American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)] - Parameter: Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol
Category: Cardiovascular & Lipidology
- **Role**: Often termed "bad cholesterol" because particles infiltrate endothelial walls, oxidize, and contribute to atherosclerotic plaque formation.
- **Optimal**: < 100 mg/dL (or < 70 mg/dL for patients with established cardiovascular disease)
- **Near/Above Optimal**: 100 - 129 mg/dL

chunks.title: Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content:
h established cardiovascular disease)
- **Near/Above Optimal**: 100 - 129 mg/dL
- **Borderline High**: 130 - 159 mg/dL
- **High**: 160 - 189 mg/dL
- **Very High**: >= 190 mg/dL
- **Clinical Significance**: Elevated LDL represents a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor. Initial management typically emphasizes dietary adjustments (reducing saturated/trans fats), regular aerobic exercise, and smoking cessation.

chunks.title: Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content: reducing saturated/trans fats), regular aerobic exercise, and smoking cessation. If risk remains elevated, clinicians evaluate statin therapy based on overall 10-year cardiovascular risk calculators.

chunks.title: High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL) Cholesterol Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content:
[American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)] - Parameter: High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL) Cholesterol
Category: Cardiovascular & Lipidology
- **Role**: Termed "good cholesterol" for mediating reverse cholesterol transport, shuttling excess cholesterol from peripheral arteries back to the liver for hepatic clearance.
- **Protective Levels**: >= 60 mg/dL
- **Higher Risk / Low Levels**: < 40 mg/dL (men), < 50 mg/dL (women)

chunks.title: Triglycerides Reference
chunks.source: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.organization: American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks.content:
[American Heart Association (AHA) & Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)] - Parameter: Triglycerides
Category: Cardiovascular & Lipidology
- **Normal**: < 150 mg/dL
- **Borderline High**: 150 - 199 mg/dL
- **High**: 200 - 499 mg/dL
- **Very High (Critical Alert)**: >= 500 mg/dL (increases the acute risk of acute pancreatitis and warrants prompt clinical review).

chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)] - Parameter: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
Category: Hepatology and Nephrology
- **Biological Role**: Intracellular enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism. ALT is predominantly concentrated in hepatocytes; AST is found in liver, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, and kidneys.
- **Typical Reference Range**: ALT: 7 - 56 U/L; AST: 10 - 40 U/L (lab specific).

chunks.title: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
**Typical Reference Range**: ALT: 7 - 56 U/L; AST: 10 - 40 U/L (lab specific).
- **Elevated Values**:
  - *Mild-to-moderate elevation (2x to 5x upper limit)*: Frequently indicates nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MASLD), chronic medication effects (e.g., statins, acetaminophen, NSAIDs), moderate alcohol consumption, or chronic viral hepatitis.

chunks.title: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
etaminophen, NSAIDs), moderate alcohol consumption, or chronic viral hepatitis.
  - *Marked elevation (>10x to 20x upper limit)*: Signals acute hepatocellular necrosis, acute viral hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), or toxin-induced injury. Prompt medical evaluation is required.

chunks.title: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) & Total Bilirubin Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)] - Parameter: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) & Total Bilirubin
Category: Hepatology and Nephrology
- **ALP**: Found in biliary duct epithelium and bone. Elevation with normal ALT/AST may reflect biliary obstruction, cholestasis, or bone turnover.
- **Bilirubin**: Breakdown product of heme. Hyperbilirubinemia may cause jaundice (yellowing of sclera/skin), tea-colored urine, or acholic stools.

## Kidney Function Tests (KFT / Renal Panel)

chunks.title: Serum Creatinine Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)] - Parameter: Serum Creatinine
Category: Hepatology and Nephrology
- **Biological Role**: Metabolic byproduct of muscle creatine breakdown. Excreted almost entirely via glomerular filtration without substantial tubular reabsorption.
- **Typical Reference Range**: 0.6 - 1.2 mg/dL (varies by age, sex, and muscular body surface area).

chunks.title: Serum Creatinine Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
Range**: 0.6 - 1.2 mg/dL (varies by age, sex, and muscular body surface area).
- **Elevated Creatinine**: Reflects diminished glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Acute increases can occur secondary to severe dehydration (prerenal azotemia), urinary outflow obstruction, nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides), or intrinsic renal parenchymal injury.

chunks.title: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)] - Parameter: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
Category: Hepatology and Nephrology
- **Typical Reference Range**: 7 - 20 mg/dL.
- **BUN/Creatinine Ratio**: An elevated ratio (>20:1) frequently points to prerenal dehydration or upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

chunks.title: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus) & National Kidney Foundation (NKF)] - Parameter: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)
Category: Hepatology and Nephrology
- **Normal**: >= 90 mL/min/1.73m^2.
- **Mild reduction**: 60 - 89 mL/min/1.73m^2.
- **Moderate to Severe reduction**: < 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 for over 3 months signifies chronic kidney disease (CKD), requiring nephrological consultation.

chunks.title: Nephrology and Urology Overview
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
# Routine Urinalysis Reference Guidelines

**Source Organization**: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
**URL**: https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/urinalysis/
**Category**: Nephrology and Urology
**Last Reviewed**: 2024

## Overview
A routine urinalysis is a diagnostic physical, chemical, and microscopic examination of urine. It serves to detect metabolic conditions, renal parenchymal diseases, and urinary tract infections.

## Key Parameters

chunks.title: Leukocyte Esterase and Nitrites Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)] - Parameter: Leukocyte Esterase and Nitrites
Category: Nephrology and Urology
- **Significance**: Leukocyte esterase indicates the presence of white blood cells (pyuria). Nitrites are produced by Gram-negative bacteria (such as E. coli) that reduce dietary nitrate.
- **Normal**: Negative.

chunks.title: Leukocyte Esterase and Nitrites Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
bacteria (such as E. coli) that reduce dietary nitrate.
- **Normal**: Negative.
- **Positive Findings**: Highly suggestive of a urinary tract infection (UTI). When accompanied by dysuria, frequency, pelvic pain, or systemic symptoms like fever and chills, prompt medical evaluation and potential urine culture are recommended.

chunks.title: Urine Protein (Albumin) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)] - Parameter: Urine Protein (Albumin)
Category: Nephrology and Urology
- **Normal**: Negative or Trace (< 15 mg/dL).
- **Abnormal (1+ to 4+ or persistent proteinuria)**: Transient benign proteinuria can occur with strenuous exercise, dehydration, orthostatic changes, or acute fever. Persistent proteinuria is an early hallmark of glomerular barrier disruption (diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis) and warrants nephrological follow-up.

chunks.title: Blood / Red Blood Cells (Hematuria) Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)] - Parameter: Blood / Red Blood Cells (Hematuria)
Category: Nephrology and Urology
- **Normal**: Negative or < 3 RBCs per high power field.
- **Abnormal (Microscopic or Gross Hematuria)**: May stem from benign causes (vigorous exercise, contamination during menstruation) or pathology including nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), infection, trauma, or urothelial neoplasms. Must be discussed with a healthcare provider for formal evaluation.

chunks.title: Urine Glucose & Ketones Reference
chunks.source: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)
chunks.content:
[National Institutes of Health (NIH MedlinePlus)] - Parameter: Urine Glucose & Ketones
Category: Nephrology and Urology
- **Normal**: Negative.
- **Positive**: Glucosuria occurs when serum glucose exceeds renal threshold (~180 mg/dL). Ketonuria signals rapid fat breakdown, seen in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), prolonged fasting, or extreme ketogenic dieting.
